headings.title: Introduction to Paediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)
headings.content: Paediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) is an intensive, evidence-based training program designed for healthcare providers who respond to emergencies involving infants and children. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding PALS is critical because paediatric emergencies require rapid, systematic assessment and precise interventions that differ significantly from adult care. PALS emphasizes the prevention of arrest through early recognition and management of respiratory distress, respiratory failure, and various forms of shock. The ultimate goal of PALS is to improve outcomes and survival rates in critically ill or injured children by utilizing a team-oriented approach, effective communication, and standardized algorithms. Throughout your nursing career, mastering these concepts will empower you to act decisively during high-stress clinical scenarios, ensuring that young patients receive timely, high-quality care that bridges the gap between basic life support and advanced critical care interventions.

headings.title: Anatomical and Physiological Differences in Children
headings.content: When providing nursing care to paediatric patients, it is vital to recognize that infants and children are not merely small adults. Their anatomical and physiological differences profoundly influence their response to illness and injury. For instance, a child's head is proportionally larger and heavier, and their airway is narrower, shorter, and more easily obstructed by secretions or improper positioning. The tongue is larger relative to the oral cavity, and the larynx is more anterior and cephalad. Physiologically, infants and young children have a high metabolic rate and consume oxygen at a much faster rate than adults, making them prone to rapid hypoxia. Furthermore, children rely heavily on an increased heart rate rather than stroke volume to maintain cardiac output; consequently, bradycardia is an ominous sign of impending cardiac arrest in paediatrics. Their compliant chest walls also transmit forces easily to internal organs, but chest compressions require careful technique to prevent trauma. Recognizing these unique traits allows Nigerian nurses to anticipate deterioration and intervene proactively.

headings.title: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT)
headings.content: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) is a rapid, tool-free assessment tool used by healthcare providers to form an initial general impression of a child's clinical condition within seconds. It relies entirely on visual and auditory cues without touching the patient, helping nurses quickly categorize the child as stable, in respiratory distress, in shock, or experiencing central nervous system dysfunction. The PAT consists of three distinct sides: Appearance, Work of Breathing, and Circulation to the Skin. 'Appearance' evaluates the child's muscle tone, interactivity, consolability, look/gaze, and speech or cry (often remembered via the TICLS mnemonic). 'Work of Breathing' assesses abnormal breath sounds, abnormal positioning, retractions, and tachypnoea. 'Circulation to the Skin' looks for pallor, mottling, or cyanosis. By evaluating these three components together, the nurse can instantly determine if the patient is suffering from primary respiratory problems, shock, brain injury, or cardiopulmonary failure, guiding immediate lifesaving priorities.

headings.title: High-Quality Basic Life Support (BLS) for Infants and Children
headings.content: High-quality Basic Life Support (BLS) is the foundation of successful resuscitation for infants and children in cardiac arrest. As a nursing student, you must master the critical components of BLS: compression rate, depth, recoil, and minimizing interruptions. For infants (under one year) and children (from one year to puberty), chest compressions must be performed at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. The recommended depth is at least one-third of the anteroposterior diameter of the chest, which translates to approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches) for infants and 5 cm (2 inches) for children. Complete chest recoil is essential to allow the heart to refill between compressions. For a single rescuer, the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2, whereas for two or more healthcare rescuers, a ratio of 15:2 is utilized. In infants, two rescuers use the two thumb-encircling hands technique, which generates superior blood flow compared to the two-finger technique. Minimizing interruptions in chest compressions is paramount to preserving coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure throughout the resuscitation effort.

headings.title: Airway Management and Ventilation Strategies
headings.content: Effective airway management and ventilation strategies are crucial in preventing paediatric cardiac arrest, as most paediatric arrests stem from progressive asphyxia. Nurses must be proficient in opening the airway using the head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver (or jaw-thrust maneuver if cervical spine injury is suspected). Basic airway adjuncts, such as oropharyngeal airways (OPAs) and nasopharyngeal airways (NPAs), help maintain airway patency; however, OPAs must be sized correctly and inserted carefully to avoid trauma to the delicate paediatric palate. When delivering positive pressure ventilation using a bag-valve-mask (BVM) device, nurses must ensure an airtight seal using the 'E-C clamp' technique. Delivering excessive tidal volume or ventilating too rapidly can cause gastric inflation, impede diaphragmatic descent, and increase the risk of aspiration and barotrauma. Advanced airway placement, such as endotracheal intubation or supraglottic airway insertion, may be required for definitive airway control, requiring precise tube sizing based on age or length-based resuscitation tapes like the Broselow tape.

headings.title: Recognition and Management of Respiratory Emergencies
headings.content: Respiratory emergencies represent the most common precursor to cardiac arrest in children. Recognizing the spectrum from mild respiratory distress to respiratory failure is an essential competency for nurses. Respiratory distress is characterized by compensatory mechanisms such as tachypnoea, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and grunting, while the child maintains adequate gas exchange and normal mental status. If these compensatory mechanisms fail, the child progresses to respiratory failure, marked by inadequate ventilation and/or oxygenation, bradycardia, lethargy, cyanosis, and head bobbing. Common underlying causes in Nigerian paediatric populations include acute severe asthma, bronchiolitis, croup, foreign body airway obstruction, and lower respiratory tract infections such as severe pneumonia. Management involves ensuring a patent airway, administering supplemental oxygen, positioning the child in a position of comfort, and delivering specific targeted therapies (e.g., bronchodilators for asthma or epinephrine for croup). In severe cases, assisted ventilation with a BVM or advanced airway management becomes life-saving.

headings.title: Recognition and Management of Shock States
headings.content: Shock is a critical clinical condition characterized by inadequate tissue perfusion to meet cellular metabolic demands. In children, shock can be classified into four main categories: hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive. Hypovolemic shock, often caused by gastroenteritis, dehydration, or hemorrhage, is the most common form globally. Distributive shock (e.g., anaphylactic, septic, or neurogenic) features inappropriate vasodilation and maldistribution of blood flow. Cardiogenic shock stems from poor myocardial function (e.g., congenital heart disease, myocarditis), while obstructive shock involves physical impairment to blood flow (e.g., tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade). A vital concept in paediatric shock is recognizing compensated shock, where blood pressure remains within normal limits due to intense vasoconstriction and tachycardia, versus decompensated shock, where perfusion fails and hypotension ensues. Because children can compensate remarkably well before their blood pressure crashes, nurses must look for subtle signs of poor perfusion, such as delayed capillary refill time, cool extremities, weak peripheral pulses, and altered mental status, and initiate rapid fluid resuscitation or inotropic support.

headings.title: Pediatric Cardiac Arrest Algorithms and Rhythm Disturbance Management
headings.content: When a child suffers cardiac arrest, immediate initiation of high-quality BLS is the single most important intervention. Paediatric cardiac arrest rhythms are categorized primarily into non-shockable rhythms (Asystole and Pulseless Electrical Activity - PEA) and shockable rhythms (Ventricular Fibrillation - VF and Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia - pVT). If a shockable rhythm is identified via manual defibrillator or AED, a shock of 2 J/kg is delivered immediately for the first shock, and subsequent shocks should be at least 4 J/kg. For non-shockable rhythms, high-quality chest compressions and early administration of epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1:10,000 solution) every 3 to 5 minutes are essential. Identifying and treating reversible causes—known as the H's and T's (Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion acidosis, Hypoglycemia, Hypo/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade cardiac, Toxins, Thrombosis pulmonary/coronary)—is critical to successfully restoring a perfusing rhythm.

headings.title: Post-Resuscitation Care
headings.content: Post-resuscitation care begins immediately after the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and focuses on optimizing ventilation, oxygenation, perfusion, and neurological recovery. Nigerian nurses must monitor and manage the child's ABCs meticulously to prevent secondary brain injury and recurrent arrest. Ventilation and oxygenation should be titrated to target normal age-appropriate blood gas values, avoiding both hypoxia and hyperoxia (which causes cerebral vasoconstriction and oxidative injury). Hemodynamic stability must be maintained through fluid management and, if necessary, inotropic or vasoactive infusions (e.g., epinephrine or dopamine) to treat post-cardiac arrest myocardial dysfunction and hypotension. Temperature management is also critical; fever must be aggressively treated, and targeted temperature management (normothermia or therapeutic hypothermia) may be implemented depending on institutional guidelines. Continuous monitoring of neurological status, blood glucose, and renal function ensures comprehensive care during this vulnerable recovery phase.
